blocks.text: An ostrich is a bird, but it never flies. It is too big and too heavy to lift off the ground. Instead, the ostrich runs. It can run faster than any other bird on land. blocks.prompt: The Bird That Gave Up Flying
blocks.text: Long ago, the ancestors of the ostrich could fly. Somewhere along the way, their family stopped. Flying costs a huge amount of energy, and it keeps a bird small. On the wide open grasslands of Africa, there was another way to stay safe: get big, and get fast. So the ostrich got big. A grown male can stand nine feet tall and weigh more than 250 pounds, which is taller than a door and heavier than most grown men. Its wings are still there, but they are far too small to lift all that weight. Instead, the ostrich runs. It can hit 43 miles per hour, which is faster than any other bird can run and faster than most horses. A single stride can cover sixteen feet of ground. When it needs to turn, it throws out its wings like a pair of sails and swings around without slowing down. If running does not work, the ostrich has one more answer. It kicks. Its legs are strong enough, and its toe claws sharp enough, that a lion will think twice.

blocks.prompt: Everything You Heard About the Ostrich Is Probably Wrong
blocks.text: You have probably heard that an ostrich buries its head in the sand when it is scared. It does not. It never has. No one has ever filmed it, because it does not happen. The idea is old. Almost two thousand years ago, a Roman writer named Pliny the Elder claimed that ostriches think their whole body is hidden when they push their head into a bush. He was wrong, but he was widely read, and the picture stuck. It has outlasted the empire that produced it. The story does have a real animal behind it, though. An ostrich nest is not a basket in a tree. It is a shallow pit scraped into the dirt. Several times a day a parent leans down, pushes its beak into the pit, and turns the eggs so they warm evenly. From a distance, across shimmering heat, a bird with its head down in a hole looks exactly like a bird with its head in the sand. There is a second habit that feeds the myth. An ostrich that has been spotted by something dangerous will sometimes drop flat to the ground and stretch its neck straight out along the dirt. Its head and neck are a dusty pink and its body is a low gray lump. Lying still, it stops looking like a nine foot bird and starts looking like a mound of earth. So the ostrich is not hiding from danger by refusing to see it. It is doing the opposite. Those enormous eyes, the largest of any animal on land, are watching the whole time, waiting for the moment to stand up and run.

blocks.prompt: Built for the Open Ground
blocks.text: Every part of an ostrich is an answer to the same question: how do you survive on flat, open ground where there is nowhere to hide? Start with the eyes. An ostrich eye is about two inches across, the largest of any animal that lives on land, and it sits on a neck that can hold it seven feet above the grass. That combination turns the bird into a watchtower. It spots a predator crossing the plain long before the predator is close enough to matter. The eye is so large that it is bigger than the ostrich's own brain, a fact people love to repeat as an insult. It is not an insult. It is a trade. Out on the savanna, seeing early is worth more than thinking hard. Next, the legs. An ostrich foot has two toes, and no other bird on Earth has fewer than three. One toe is broad and carries a thick claw. The other is smaller and steadies the bird as it turns. Fewer toes means less foot slapping the ground, and less foot means a longer, cheaper stride. The result is a bird that can reach 43 miles per hour and hold about 30 for half an hour without stopping. Almost nothing that hunts it can do that twice. Then the stomach. Ostriches have no teeth, so they swallow stones. The stones collect in a muscular pouch called the gizzard, where they grind up tough grass, seeds, and leaves. An adult may carry two pounds of gravel inside it at all times, which sounds absurd until you remember that it is doing the job your molars do. Even the nest is built for open country. Ostriches share one. A dominant female scrapes a pit in the dirt and lays her eggs, and other females add theirs around the edge. She keeps her own in the warm center and lets the outer eggs take the risk. Then the parents split the shift. The female, dusty brown and gray, sits through the day and vanishes against the dry ground. The male, black with white wings, sits through the night and vanishes against the dark. Nothing here is an accident. A bird this size cannot hide, so it watches, runs, eats anything, and hands the odds to somebody else's eggs.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Struthio camelus, the largest living bird
Its feathers lack the hooks that make flight feathers stiff
Ostrich farming began in South Africa in the 1860s
By 1913 feathers were among South Africa's largest exports
The feather palaces of Oudtshoorn still stand
The market collapsed in 1914 and never returned

blocks.prompt: Forever Grounded: The Feather That Built a Town
blocks.text: A flight feather is a machine. A stiff central shaft runs down the middle, and off it branch hundreds of barbs. Each barb carries rows of tiny barbules, and the barbules carry microscopic hooks that latch onto the barbules of the neighboring barb. Zipped together, the whole surface locks into a smooth, taut vane that can shove against air without letting it through. That vane is the reason birds own the sky. The ostrich threw the machine away. Once its ancestors stopped flying, there was no longer any pressure to maintain the hooks, and evolution does not pay for tools nobody uses. The barbules of an ostrich feather have no working hooks. The barbs never zip. They hang loose and separate from the shaft, and the feather droops into a soft, weightless plume that could not push air if the bird's life depended on it. For flying, it is junk. For being looked at, it is perfect. The males use their black and white plumes in a courtship display, dropping to the ground and rocking their wings from side to side like someone shaking out a rug. A feather that has stopped flying is free to become beautiful. Then people noticed. In the second half of the nineteenth century, European and American fashion decided that a woman's hat was not finished without ostrich plumes, and the bigger the better. The demand was enormous, and the supply was a wild bird in Africa. So farmers built an industry around it. In the Little Karoo, in a dry valley town called Oudtshoorn, ostrich farming turned into a boom. Farmers who had been scratching a living out of hard ground suddenly held a crop that grew back every eight months and sold by weight. They built enormous sandstone houses with turrets and imported tiles and stained glass. People called them feather palaces, and the name was not entirely kind. By 1913, ostrich feathers were among South Africa's largest exports, sitting on the same list as gold, diamonds, and wool. Then it ended, and it ended fast. In 1914 the war closed the shipping lanes that carried feathers to London and New York. At the same time, fashion moved on. Motor cars were open at the top, and a hat crowned with two feet of plume did not survive a drive at speed. Hair went short. Hats went small. Within months the price of a feather fell by more than ninety percent and it never recovered. Farmers who had been wealthy in the spring were ruined by the autumn. The birds were turned loose or sold for almost nothing. The feather palaces of Oudtshoorn are still standing today, most of them restored, some of them museums, all of them monuments to a fortune that evaporated in a single season. Here is what is worth noticing. The feather was valuable for exactly the reason it was useless. The hooks failed, the vane fell apart, and that ruined plume happened to match what a few thousand people in distant cities wanted to wear on their heads. The bird did not change. The feather did not change. The fashion changed, and an entire economy went with it. The ostrich had already learned that lesson long before Oudtshoorn did: nothing keeps a thing it has no use for.
